Commentary.Commentary: We are back for the chase! The players are already out in the middle now. Evin Lewis and Johnson Charles are the two openers for the West Indies. Luke Wood to start proceedings with the ball. Here we go...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

Not much went right for the Windies with the ball, as they were taken apart with ease. Their pace attack lacked penetration and struggled for control, allowing England's batters to dominate from the outset. The spin duo of Akeal Hosein and Gudakesh Motie did manage to pick up a wicket each, but by then the damage was well underway. A surprising move saw Sherfane Rutherford thrown into the attack, and he provided a rare bright spot by dismissing Buttler early, perhaps preventing an even steeper climb. However, in a disappointing turn of events, he picked up a hamstring injury, and we are unsure whether he will come out to bat or not, which would be a big loss if he cannot. Now, it’s time for the Windies to flex their Caribbean muscle with the bat. If there’s any team that can pull off a chase of this magnitude, it’s them. Stick around for what promises to be a thrilling pursuit.

Already 2-0 up in the series, England showed no signs of easing off. Their openers, Ben Duckett and Jamie Smith, came out firing on all cylinders, showing no mercy to the bowlers. Boundaries rained in every direction as they stormed to 83 runs in the Powerplay. Both openers brought up rapid half-centuries and shared a blistering 120-run stand for the first wicket. At the 10-over mark, they were cruising at 135/1- their highest-ever score at that stage in a T20I. Duckett fell short of a well-earned century, departing for a scintillating 84 off just 46 balls, but the momentum never dipped. Jos Buttler, Harry Brook, and Jacob Bethell - the Triple B's each chipped in with explosive cameos. Brook and Bethell combined brilliantly to add 70 more runs, propelling England close to that imposing 250-run mark.

Be it Tests, ODIs, or T20Is, England’s batting philosophy rests on a single, ruthless credo - relentless aggression. Losing a wicket barely ruffles them as each incoming batter brandishes the same fearless intent, and that collective mindset makes them a formidable outfit. Every player understands his role, embraces risk, and more often than not reaps the rewards. Tonight was yet another masterclass, as they blazed their way to 248, England’s second-highest total in this format.

In case you missed it, Nicholas Pooran has announced his retirement from international cricket. He had initially asked for a break from the current series after his IPL stint, but his decision to retire has come as a surprise. Pooran finishes his career as the West Indies player with the most T20I appearances and the highest run tally in the format. His departure is a big setback for the Men in Maroon, especially with the 2026 T20 World Cup ahead.

As we look over both batting lineups, the prospect of a deluge of boundaries looms big once again, with both sides stacked with power hitters capable of launching the ball over the ropes at will. Can the Windies finally come back and win a game on this challenging tour? Or will the hosts find a way to blow them away once again, completing a perfect series sweep? We'll find out. Stay tuned for the toss and team updates.

On the other hand, the West Indies have had a difficult time on this tour, still looking for their first win against England following a clean sweep in the ODIs and two T20I defeats. In the second T20I, the men in maroon put up a brilliant batting performance, but their bowling has been a significant cause for concern as it proved expensive against the aggressive English batting. They have some of the most well-known players in T20 cricket, but far too frequently, individual excellence hasn't translated into team success.

For England, they are riding high on confidence, as in the second T20I, their deep and dynamic batting lineup chased down the target of 197 runs with nine balls and four wickets to spare. Their deep batting lineup, with rejuvenated Jos Buttler supported by the likes of Harry Brook and Tom Banton, has been relentless. The hosts will be eager to complete a clean sweep and further cement their status as one of the premier white-ball teams in world cricket.

Hello and a warm welcome to everyone as we are here at the picturesque Utilita Bowl in Southampton for the third and final T20 International of the three-match series between England and the West Indies. Following their dominant performance in the ODI series, the hosts have already secured an unassailable 2-0 lead in the T20I series and will be aiming for a clean sweep. Meanwhile, the visitors will be playing to salvage pride and find some much-needed momentum before they depart for Ireland.
... MATCH DAY ...

A dominant England side will be aiming for a clean sweep when they take on a dispirited West Indies in the third and final T20I of the series at the Rose Bowl in Southampton. Having already secured the series with convincing victories in the first two matches, the hosts are riding a wave of momentum, leaving the visitors with the daunting task of salvaging some pride from a tour that has so far been winless. England, under the leadership of new white-ball skipper Harry Brook, have been clinical in all departments. Their batting has been explosive, their bowling incisive, and their fielding sharp, a combination that the West Indies have struggled to counter. The preceding 3-0 whitewash in the ODI series has been followed by two comprehensive wins in the shortest format, underlining England's superiority in home conditions. The second encounter in Bristol was a higher-scoring affair, with the West Indies posting a competitive 196/6. However, England's deep and dynamic batting line-up, a hallmark of their white-ball prowess, rose to the occasion, chasing down the target with nine balls and four wickets to spare. The victory, orchestrated by contributions throughout the order, highlighted the gulf between the two sides in pressure situations. The series now moves to the picturesque Rose Bowl in Southampton, a venue known for its balanced contest between bat and ball. The pitch here tends to be on the drier side, which can make stroke-play more challenging as the game progresses. Spinners are expected to come into play, particularly in the second innings, with the surface offering some grip and turn. he hosts are a well-oiled machine, brimming with confidence and depth. The batting unit has been formidable. Jos Buttler has been in sublime touch, leading from the front with scores of 96 and 47. The likes of Harry Brook, Tom Banton, and the explosive Jacob Bethell have provided crucial middle-order firepower. The bowling attack has successfully blended experience and new talent. Left-armer Luke Wood, Player of the Match in the second T20I for his crucial spell of 2/25, has been a revelation. The veteran leg-spinner Adil Rashid remains a constant threat, while the return of Liam Dawson has added another potent spin option. With the series won, England might be tempted to give opportunities to other members of their squad, but their relentless pursuit of victory is unlikely to diminish. The men in maroon have been a shadow of the T20 force they are known to be. While there have been flashes of individual brilliance, they have failed to click as a collective. The batting has been heavily reliant on captain Shai Hope (49 in the second T20I) and Johnson Charles (47). The much-vaunted power-hitting of Rovman Powell has been sporadic, and the rest of the batting has lacked consistency. Their bowling has been a significant cause for concern, proving expensive against the aggressive English batting. Senior pacers like Alzarri Joseph have been unable to contain the run flow, and the spinners have struggled to exert control in the middle overs. For the final match, the West Indies need their star players to stand up and deliver a complete team performance, turning their individual potential into a match-winning effort.
